*& Carries finished translations from system to system, place by place.
* The vocabulary route matches on the source text, and that is where it breaks.
* The customer system has no Russian, so the key would have to be English, and
* English collapses distinctions the Russian kept: "In Review" stands for both
* "В проверке" and "На проверке", which were translated differently and both
* correctly. One vocabulary row cannot hold both.
* The object does not collapse. GRFN_AMSTATUS value 0002 has exactly one
* Ukrainian text and GRFN_WI_STATUS value 0003 has exactly one, and they are
* allowed to differ. So this report carries the pairs themselves - object,
* field, sub key, text - and matches nothing. There is no vocabulary here, no
* lookup, no ambiguity, and nothing to decide.
* It also removes the detection problem. In the customer system Ukrainian was
* supplemented from English, so every UK text equals its EN text and nothing
* looks untranslated. Import does not look: it overwrites the target-language
* text of every place named in the file.
* What it does not fix: the inconsistency travels with the translation. If SAP
* rendered one English term two ways, both ways arrive. Settling on one wording
* is a separate pass, afterwards, and a question of terminology rather than of
* File format is CSV as Excel expects it: semicolon separated, UTF-8 with a byte
* order mark, one record per line, a field quoted when it contains a semicolon
* or a quote, and an internal quote doubled. A text containing a line break is
* refused by the export and named, rather than written out to break the file
